titulo.texto: Traditional Gauze Huipil with Curved Weave from Cuetzalan

frase_gancho.texto: A huipil so fine it seems made of mist.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the textiles of the mountains, we move on to those of Oaxaca. Look for a dark velvet outfit embroidered with large, colorful flowers and a white lace that forms a kind of frame around the face.

guion_corto.texto: This huipil comes from Cuetzalan, in the northern mountains of Puebla, and it was woven by Nahua women. It is made of very fine white cotton on a backstrap loom, using a gauze or openwork technique that leaves tiny gaps and makes the cloth light and almost transparent, like the mist of the mountains. On the chest it carries embroidered birds, flowers and geometric figures. It is worn at festivals and weddings, together with a headdress of colored wool. Look closely at the weave: it seems impossible that this is cloth. Every thread was counted, crossed and adjusted by hand, and the result is a garment of extraordinary delicacy.

guion_largo.texto:
When Cuetzalan wakes wrapped in mist, the clothing of its women seems made of that very air. The gauze huipil is a white garment, light, almost transparent, and for that very reason difficult to make. More than a blouse, it is a piece of engineering made with thread.

Notice how it is achieved. On the backstrap loom, the weaver crosses the threads in a special way to leave tiny gaps between them. This technique is called gauze or openwork weaving. The gaps make the cloth cool and light, but also more fragile, so every thread must be tensioned with precision. A mistake shows immediately.

Remember the huipil in the entrance hall of the upper floor: two or three panels sewn together, with nothing cut from the cloth. This one follows the same rule, with extraordinary fineness. And the cotton it is woven from was, in the time of the Mexica, one of the most valuable tributes they received, in the form of blankets.

On that vaporous background are the embroideries. Birds, flowers and geometric figures appear, woven or embroidered with thread of the same color, so that the design is seen through relief and shadow. It is a discreet elegance: it does not shine, it only hints. You have already seen the [Otomí quechquémitl](mna_s15_quechquemitl_otomi), full of colors; this huipil plays with the opposite, with the subtlety of white on white.

The garment is not worn alone. At festivals, the women of Cuetzalan also wear a wool headdress, called maxtahual, woven in red and green and braided with the hair. It is said that its shape recalls a serpent or the radiance of the Sun, and it is a source of pride for whoever wears it. Imagine the whole ensemble: white, red and green, among cobblestone streets and mist.

The name of the place also tells a story. Cuetzalan is usually explained as “place of quetzals,” and you have already seen that this bird is present in the crown dance. It is the same land that dresses its women in fine cloth and its men in crowns and flying costumes. The mountains have given Mexico a culture of the fine, the airy and the luminous.

At traditional weddings, the bride usually wears one of her best huipils, and sometimes her mother’s or grandmother’s is passed down. And in Cuetzalan there are cooperatives of Nahua women who sell their textiles and defend them with pride.

Every year, Cuetzalan celebrates a huipil and coffee fair, and it is the women who show their cloth, their embroidery and their techniques. It is a way of making the craft seen and valued. A huipil like this one can take months to make, and that time is often not paid enough. That is why it matters to buy them directly from those who weave them.

Before moving on, stop for a moment and look at the cloth against the light, if you can. You will notice how the air passes between the threads. It is the best lesson in what “delicacy” means: a cloth that weighs nothing, that hides nothing, and yet withstands use and the passing of the years.

texto: Look at the tiny gaps in the gauze weave
Find the embroidered birds and flowers, white on white
Compare the cloth with mist: how transparent is it?

texto.Region: Northern Sierra of Puebla (Cuetzalan del Progreso / Tzinacapan)
texto.Technique/Material: Cotton woven on a backstrap loom (gauze and curved warp technique) and embroidery
texto.Function: Ceremonial formal attire, traditional weddings and patron saint festivities

texto.pregunta: Myth: White huipils are plain garments that take little work.
texto.respuesta: Reality: A gauze huipil demands a very precise technique and can take months to weave. The simplicity of the color hides an enormous difficulty.
